Regression coefficient summary table

Source: R/table_regression.R
table_regression.Rd

Publication-ready coefficient table from one or more fitted regression models: linear and generalized linear models, robust, instrumental-variable, quantile and fixed-effects estimators, mixed-effects and GEE models, ordinal, multinomial, count and two-part models, survival models, survey-design fits, additive, beta-regression and sample-selection models, and Bayesian fits, 39 model classes listed by table_regression_models(). Several fits, of one class or of several, go side by side in one table. For lm and glm, it supports standardized coefficients (\(\beta\)), average marginal effects (AME), partial effect sizes (\(f^2\) / \(\eta^2\) / \(\omega^2\) and partial F for lm; partial \(\chi^2\) or partial F for glm), pseudo-\(R^2\) and deviance \(R^2\) (glm), and a full vocabulary of variance estimators (classical / HC* / cluster-robust with Satterthwaite-corrected df / bootstrap / jackknife). glm covers binomial / poisson / Gamma / inverse.gaussian / quasi families with any link.

Usage

table_regression(
  models,
  vcov = "classical",
  cluster = NULL,
  ci_level = 0.95,
  ci_method = c("wald", "profile", "boot_percentile", "hdi"),
  boot_n = 1000L,
  tau = NULL,
  at_time = NULL,
  standardized = c("none", "refit", "posthoc", "basic", "smart", "pseudo"),
  exponentiate = FALSE,
  ame_type = c("slope", "unit", "sd"),
  partial_type = c("II", "III"),
  p_adjust = "none",
  show_columns = NULL,
  keep = NULL,
  drop = NULL,
  show_intercept = TRUE,
  show_thresholds = TRUE,
  show_components = TRUE,
  intercept_position = c("first", "last"),
  factor_layout = c("grouped", "flat"),
  reference_style = c("row", "annotation", "footer", "none"),
  reference_label = NULL,
  show_fit_stats = NULL,
  fit_stats_layout = c("first_col", "merged"),
  layout = c("columns", "stacked"),
  show_re = TRUE,
  re_scale = c("sd", "variance"),
  re_columns = c("est", "se", "ci"),
  re_test = c("none", "lrt", "rlrt"),
  re_ci = c("wald", "profile"),
  model_labels = NULL,
  outcome_labels = NULL,
  stars = FALSE,
  nested = FALSE,
  digits = 2L,
  p_digits = 3L,
  effect_size_digits = 2L,
  fit_digits = 2L,
  ic_digits = 1L,
  decimal_mark = ".",
  align = c("decimal", "center", "right"),
  padding = 0L,
  labels = getOption("spicy.var_labels", FALSE),
  note_labels = NULL,
  title = NULL,
  note = NULL,
  note_add = NULL,
  output = c("default", "data.frame", "long", "tinytable", "gt", "flextable", "excel",
    "clipboard", "word"),
  excel_path = NULL,
  excel_sheet = NULL,
  clipboard_delim = "\t",
  word_path = NULL,
  word_template = NULL,
  style = NULL
)

Arguments

models

A fitted model object, or a list of such fits (named or unnamed; classes may be mixed). Single fits are auto-promoted to a 1-element list. A broad set of model classes is supported – linear / generalized linear (lm, glm, MASS::glm.nb), mixed-effects (lmer, lme, glmmTMB), survival (coxph, survreg), ordinal (polr, clm, and the cumulative-link mixed models ordinal::clmm and glmmTMB with family = glmmTMB::ordinal()), mgcv::gam/bam, betareg, mlogit, survey::svyglm, rms (ols/lrm/cph/Glm), and Bayesian (rstanarm/brms), among others. An unsupported class raises spicy_unsupported. Raw data + formula is not accepted – fit-only API.

vcov

Variance-covariance estimator: "classical", "HC0"-"HC5", "CR0"-"CR3", "bootstrap", or "jackknife". A scalar is recycled to all models; a list (one string per model) allows mixed estimators. Default "classical". The resampling estimators (lm / glm, including MASS::glm.nb) refit each replicate on resampled rows of the fixed evaluated design; for glm.nb the dispersion parameter theta is held at its full-sample estimate (Stata's nbreg, vce(bootstrap) re-estimates it per replicate – the two conventions differ slightly). Resampling that fails on nearly every replicate raises spicy_resampling_failed rather than silently reporting a different estimator. Quantile regression (quantreg::rq) uses its own estimator family instead ("nid", the default, "iid", "ker", "rank" and "bootstrap"); see table_regression_robust. The values each class accepts are in Robust SE availability by model class. With nested = TRUE, the change test of each pair uses the same estimator (a Wald test; see Hierarchical (nested) model comparison). See Inference and standard errors.

cluster

Cluster identifier for cluster-robust variance (used when vcov is "CR0"-"CR3" or a cluster-bootstrap / cluster-jackknife). Three accepted forms (see How to specify cluster in the details):

  • Formula: ~region, ~region:year (recommended).

  • String column name: "region".

  • Atomic vector of length nobs(fit): df$region, interaction(df$region, df$year), ... (for keys derived on the fly).

For multi-model use, pass a list of one form per model (mix-and-match allowed). A bare unquoted name (cluster = region) is not column selection: it is evaluated as an ordinary variable (the vector form when region exists in the calling environment, a migration error pointing at ~region / "region" otherwise). Default NULL (no clustering).

ci_level

Confidence level for all reported CIs (B, \(\beta\), AME, partial effect sizes). Default 0.95.

ci_method

CI construction. "wald" (default) uses estimate +/- z x SE (t x SE for lm). "profile" (glm and ordinal MASS::polr / ordinal::clm) uses the profile-likelihood CI from stats::confint() – MASS::confint.glm() for glm, confint.polr() / confint.clm() for ordinal fits – asymmetric, exact for likelihood-based inference (Venables & Ripley 2002, Section 7.2, p. 198, and Section 8.4, pp. 220-221). Only the CI bounds change; estimate, SE, statistic and p-value remain Wald. For ordinal fits, see table_regression_ordinal. "profile" with lm raises spicy_invalid_input. "boot_percentile" (requires vcov = "bootstrap" for every model) replaces the coefficient CI bounds with equal-tailed percentile intervals of the bootstrap replicates (the boot::boot.ci() type = "perc" convention; Davison & Hinkley 1997, ch. 5), reusing the same resamples as the bootstrap SEs. Only the CI bounds change; estimate, SE, statistic and p-value remain Wald from the bootstrap covariance – the Stata convention (normal-based table CIs by default, percentile on request via estat bootstrap). AME and standardized-beta CIs are not covered. With exponentiate = TRUE the percentile bounds are exponentiated (percentile intervals are transformation-respecting). "hdi" (Bayesian stanreg / brmsfit fits only) replaces the default equal-tailed credible interval with the highest-density interval; see table_regression_bayesian. Requesting "hdi" for a frequentist fit, or "profile" / "boot_percentile" for a Bayesian fit, raises spicy_invalid_input.

boot_n

Number of bootstrap replicates when vcov = "bootstrap", and of the bootstrap of the RMST and risk-difference columns: a positive whole number, as in table_continuous_lm() and table_multiresponse(). Default 1000L, the default of table_continuous_lm(), which computes the same bootstrap variance. That variance, of a lm or glm fit, needs at least 10 valid replicates: a smaller boot_n is an error. Typed in a table that runs no bootstrap, it is ignored with a warning (class spicy_ignored_arg).

tau

Survival models only: the RMST horizon of the "rmst" columns, a positive time or "minmax", with no default. See table_regression_survival.

at_time

Survival models only: the landmark time of the "risk_diff" columns, a positive time, with no default. See table_regression_survival.

standardized

Standardization method for the "beta" column. One of "none" (default), "refit", "posthoc", "basic", "smart", "pseudo". "pseudo" is glm only (Menard 2011 fully-standardized); using it with lm() raises spicy_invalid_input. Supported classes: lm, glm (incl. MASS::glm.nb), the mixed engines ("refit" only; see table_regression_mixed), and fixed-effects Bayesian fits ("posthoc", "basic" and "smart" only; see table_regression_bayesian). Any other class raises spicy_unsupported_standardized rather than rendering an empty beta column. See the Standardized coefficients section.

exponentiate

Logical. When TRUE, B, the CI bounds, and the SE (delta method: SE_OR = OR x SE_log-odds) are exp()-transformed for links where the result is a ratio: logit (OR), log (IRR / RR / MR per family, generic exp(B) for other log-link families – a genuine ratio of means), and binomial / ordinal cloglog (HR; grouped-time proportional hazards, Prentice & Gloeckler 1978). For the ordinal (cumulative) cloglog model the displayed HR is exp(-B), not exp(B); see table_regression_ordinal. The statistic and p-value stay on the link scale (invariant under monotone transformation). Identity-link fits are left untouched (a spicy_ignored_arg warning fires when no model in the table exponentiates), so mixed lm + logit tables keep working. Any other link (probit, cauchit, inverse – the Gamma() default –, 1/mu^2, sqrt, ordinal loglog, ...) raises spicy_invalid_input: the exponential of such a coefficient has no ratio interpretation, and reporting it would mislabel the estimate. Report response-scale effects for those models via the AME column instead. Note that the displayed CI is the link-scale CI with exponentiated endpoints (Wald or profile per ci_method), so it is asymmetric around the ratio and cannot be reconstructed as estimate ± q × SE; the delta-method SE follows the Stata convention ([R] logistic, Methods and formulas: se(OR) = OR × se(b)) and the log-scale CI endpoints carry the uncertainty more faithfully than this SE. The footer states the SE scale and the CI asymmetry whenever an SE column is displayed. It also names what a displayed intercept estimates once exponentiated, which is no ratio: the baseline odds (logit), risk (binomial log), rate (count families, log) or mean (other log-link families) at the reference profile. Default FALSE.

ame_type

The quantity the AME columns report for a continuous predictor. "slope" (default): the average slope dY/dX, the derivative of the prediction averaged over the observations (Stata's margins, dydx()). "unit": the average change in the prediction when the predictor rises by one unit from each observation's own value. "sd": the same for a rise of one standard deviation, the unweighted standard deviation of the predictor in the estimation sample, again from each observation's own value. These are the uncentered unit and standard-deviation changes of Long and Freese (2014), averaged over the observations as in Mize, Doan and Long (2019). The step is taken on the variable as it is in the data, before any transformation the formula applies (log(x), poly(x, 2)). For the observations with the highest values, it can carry the predictor beyond the values observed: the prediction there is an extrapolation of the model. Gelman and Pardoe (2007) consider changes only in the region of support of the data. "sd" is not the "sd" shortcut of marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(), which moves every observation between the same two values, the mean minus and the mean plus half a standard deviation. For an unweighted fit and marginaleffects' default forward contrast, it equals avg_comparisons(fit, variables = list(x = sd(x))), the standard deviation taken over the rows the fit used. The three agree when the prediction is linear in the predictor (an lm without transformed terms: "unit" equals the slope, "sd" the slope times the standard deviation). Under a non-identity link they differ, the more so as the coefficient grows: with a log link and no interaction, the slope is b * mean(mu) and the change for one unit (exp(b) - 1) * mean(mu). "unit" is the quantity the sentence "one more unit of X goes with ... more of Y" describes; the slope only approximates it. Categorical, logical and 0/1 predictors are contrasts with their reference level under every value. Weighted fits average with the same weights under every value, per-category models (ordinal, multinomial) report the quantity for each category probability, and Bayesian fits summarize its draws. The table note names the quantity. The AME is averaged over the data the model was fitted on, read again from the environment of the fit when the table is built: when they have changed since (rows dropped, values recoded), the AME cells of that model stay empty, with a warning. Ignored, with a warning, when no AME column is shown.

partial_type

The hypothesis of the term-level tests and of the partial effect sizes built on them: every partial_* column ("partial_f", "partial_chi2", "partial_f2", "partial_eta2", "partial_omega2" and their intervals), for the models that have a term-level test (lm, glm, MASS::glm.nb, lmer / glmer, glmmTMB, nlme::lme). "II" (default) tests a term against the model without it and without the interactions that contain it, the convention of car::Anova(type = 2) that respects marginality: a main effect is tested as if its interactions were absent. "III" tests a term's own coefficients with every other term kept, its interactions included, the default of SPSS UNIANOVA, SAS PROC GLM and afex: a main effect is tested at the average of the levels of the factors it interacts with. The two give the same test for a term contained in no interaction. The numbers 2 and 3 (or "2" and "3"), as car::Anova(), afex and lmerTest take them, name the same two types.

A Type III test depends on how the factors are coded, so it is computed with every unordered factor (character and logical variables included) coded to sum to zero and every ordered factor by orthogonal polynomials, whatever contrasts the model was fitted with: the table shows the coefficients as fitted, and the test is that of car::Anova(type = 3) on the model refitted with contrasts = list(A = "contr.sum", ...). For lm and the mixed models it is the Wald test of the term's coefficients in that coding (the F over its df for lm, the chi-square for the mixed models, under a robust vcov too); for glm, the likelihood-ratio chi-square or the F of the refit without the term's columns. A model with an aliased coefficient (an empty cell of an interaction) has no Type III test and is refused. So is a factor fitted with a contrast matrix of fewer columns than its levels minus one, a model that does not hold the whole factor. A numeric covariate that interacts with a factor makes the Type III test of that factor a test where the covariate is 0, as in SPSS and SAS: a warning says so, and centering the covariate tests the factor at its mean. Nothing is centered for you. The note ends the definition of each partial statistic with "(Type II)" or "(Type III)", and tidy() and output = "long" carry the type in a partial_type column. Ignored, with a warning, when no partial column is shown.

p_adjust

Multiple-comparison adjustment method applied to the family of estimated coefficient p-values within each model (intercept and reference rows excluded). One of "none" (default), "holm", "hochberg", "hommel", "bonferroni", "BH" / "fdr", or "BY". Delegated to stats::p.adjust(); applied per-model and per estimate_type (B and AME p-values are adjusted independently within their own families). The tests of the smooth terms of a GAM join the B family. Active adjustments are documented in the footer (method + family size). See the Multiple-comparison adjustment section for when this is and is not appropriate.

show_columns

Character vector of tokens selecting the per-coefficient columns and their display order. Accepts atomic tokens ("b", "se", "ci", "t", "p", "df" (the degrees of freedom of each coefficient's t test, blank under a z test; refused when every test of the table is z), "beta","n", "n_events", "pd" (probability of direction, Bayesian fits only), "rhat" / "ess_bulk" / "ess_tail" / "mcse" (per-coefficient sampler diagnostics and the Monte Carlo standard error of the displayed posterior median, all-Bayesian tables only), "ame", "ame_se", "ame_ci", "ame_p", "rmst" + "rmst_se" / "rmst_ci" / "rmst_p", "risk_diff" + its _se / _ci / _p companions, "partial_f2" + "partial_f2_ci", "partial_eta2" + "partial_eta2_ci", "partial_omega2" + "partial_omega2_ci", "partial_chi2", "partial_f" (lm, and glm whose dispersion is estimated), "r2" / "adj_r2" (per-fit variance explained, lm screens)) and group tokens ("all_b", "all_b_compact", "all_b_full", "all_beta", "all_ame", "all_ame_compact", "all_f2", "all_eta2", "all_omega2"). See table_regression_tokens for the full enumeration. Default NULL selects a context-aware layout: "all_b" (single model) or "all_b_compact" (multi-model, and the single-multinomial outcome-as-columns layout, which has the same width pressure – restore CIs with atomic tokens, e.g. c("b", "se", "ci", "p")). The "p" token is always the B / beta p-value; for the AME-specific p-value use "ame_p". "none" shows the fit statistics alone, one column per model (see Fit statistics alone in table_regression_tokens).

keep

Character vector of term names or regexes. Only coefficient rows whose term name (as in stats::coef() – e.g. "wt", "cyl6", "factor(cyl)8"; the terms of an rms fit in the spelling of lm(), "cyl6" for rms's "cyl=6" and "wt:cyl6" for "wt * cyl=6") matches at least one pattern are kept. A pattern is a Perl regular expression, and one identical to a term name also selects that term as written, with no escaping ("log(bili)"). The intercept and the subordinate blocks (thresholds, random effects) are exempt from keep and drop: show_intercept, show_thresholds and show_re govern them. The smooth terms of a GAM are predictors and are not exempt: they match by their mgcv label ("s(age)", "te(bmi,ped)"), and drop = "^s\\(" removes the Smooth terms block with its note. The Error terms of a sample-selection model are coefficients of coef() and follow keep and drop under those names ("sigma", "rho", "invMillsRatio"). Mutually exclusive with drop. Filtering is a display choice; p_adjust runs against the full coefficient family before filtering. Default NULL (no filter).

drop

Character vector of regexes. Coefficient rows matching any pattern are removed, with the exemptions of keep. Mutually exclusive with keep. Default NULL.

show_intercept

Whether to display the intercept row. Default TRUE (APA convention). Hide via FALSE.

show_thresholds

Ordinal models only: TRUE (default) shows the cut-points as a Thresholds block of rows, FALSE gives them in the note. See table_regression_ordinal.

show_components

Models with secondary components only (the pscl and glmmTMB two-part and dispersion models, clm with scale =, the precision sub-model of a betareg y ~ x | z, the error terms of a sample-selection model): TRUE (default) shows the components as labeled blocks of rows, FALSE omits them. A Precision block stays on the scale of its link (log by default), under exponentiate = TRUE too. See table_regression_counts, table_regression_ordinal and table_regression_models.

intercept_position

Where to place the intercept when shown. "first" (default, APA) or "last" (Stata-style, intercept just above the fit-stats footer). Ignored when show_intercept = FALSE (with spicy_ignored_arg warning).

factor_layout

Layout of factor predictors. Applies to any categorical predictor – factor, ordered, character, or logical (R coerces the latter two to factors at fit time). Two options:

  • "grouped" (default): the variable name on its own header row ending with : (e.g., education:); each level follows as an indented sub-row with the bare level name. APA convention.

  • "flat": each non-reference dummy is one row with the <variable><level> form (e.g., educationUpper); no header, no indent. Econometrics convention.

reference_style

Rendering of factor reference levels. Four modes, distinguishing WHERE the reference information is exposed (in a row, inline, in the footer, or nowhere):

  • "row" (default): explicit row Female (ref.) with en-dashes in all stat columns (NEJM / BMJ clinical convention). reference_label controls the suffix.

  • "annotation": the row is dropped and the reference is shown inline. Under factor_layout = "grouped" the factor header reads education: [ref: Lower]; under factor_layout = "flat" the marker [vs Lower] is attached to the first non-reference dummy of each factor (subsequent dummies inherit the same reference).

  • "footer": the row is dropped and a sentence Reference categories: education = Lower; sex = Female. is added to the footer note. SAS PROC LOGISTIC / SPSS "Categorical Variables Codings" convention. Best for publication-grade dense multi-factor tables.

  • "none": the row is dropped and no reference information is displayed anywhere. The user is responsible for stating the reference convention elsewhere (article text, table caption). Under factor_layout = "flat", an informational message is emitted to flag the silent omission.

Ordered factors with AME: under R's default contr.poly, ordered factors have B coefficients named .L / .Q / .C (orthogonal polynomial trends) which have no per-level reference semantics. When "ame" is in show_columns, however, the AME block is per-level contrasts against levels()[1]. A synthetic reference row anchored on levels()[1] is therefore emitted so the reader sees the AME baseline explicitly, with the same reference_style handling as plain treatment-coded factors. The [vs <ref>] annotation in "annotation" mode is attached to the first AME row, not to the polynomial-trend rows.

reference_label

Suffix shown after the reference level in reference_style = "row" mode. NULL (default) prints "(ref.)", translated under options(spicy.language = ); a string you supply is printed as typed. Ignored by the other three modes, whose fixed wording follows the language: [ref: ...], [vs ...], and the footer line Reference categories: .... The suffix follows the level after a space, unless it opens on ,, ; or :, which attach to the level directly: a level such as T0 (2018) reads T0 (2018) (ref.); reference_label = ", ref." gives T0 (2018), ref.; reference_style = "annotation" moves the reference out of the row.

show_fit_stats

Character vector of tokens for the model-level rows below the coefficients; row order follows token order. NULL (default) resolves class-aware:

  • lm, estimatr::lm_robust(): c("nobs", "r2", "adj_r2"). estimatr::iv_robust() gets "nobs" alone, and an IV fixest::feols() neither R-squared nor AIC – the 2SLS R-squared is not the classical one. Asked for, it is the R-squared of ivreg(), on the structural residuals.

  • a logit on a binary outcome (glm or binary rms::lrm): c("nobs", "pseudo_r2_tjur", "pseudo_r2_mcfadden", "aic").

  • the other binomial, Poisson and negative binomial glm fits, polr, clm, multinom, ordinal rms::lrm: c("nobs", "pseudo_r2_mcfadden", "aic").

  • gaussian, Gamma, inverse Gaussian and Tweedie glm fits: c("nobs", "r2_deviance", "aic").

  • mixed lm + glm: the union of the two (the renderer en-dashes per cell the stat not defined for a given model class).

  • mixed-effects, survival, survey-design, Bayesian, robust and panel models: see the page of the family (Pages by model family).

Under nested = TRUE the default is extended with the class-appropriate change-stat tokens (e.g. "r2_change", "f_change" for lm). See table_regression_tokens (show_fit_stats section) and Hierarchical (nested) model comparison in the details for the full vocabulary. A token you name must have a value for at least one model of the table, or the call is refused with an error that names it (a change token also needs nested = TRUE). A token of the default that no model has is left out.

fit_stats_layout

Layout of the fit-stat values (n, R^2, AIC, ...) within each model's column group. Two options:

  • "first_col" (default): the value is placed in the FIRST numeric sub-column of each model (typically B); the model's remaining sub-columns (SE, LL, UL, p, ...) are left empty for that row. The APA Manual 7 Table 7.15 layout (p. 219).

  • "merged": the model's numeric sub-columns are merged into a single wide cell containing the fit-stat value, centered under the model spanner. Stata esttab layout / Econometrica and AER journal convention. Resolves the mixed-precision look of "first_col" (an integer n row sharing the B column with two-decimal coefficients).

excel, flextable, word and tinytable (in HTML, LaTeX and Typst) merge the cells. The markdown output of tinytable, gt (with a warning), clipboard and default (console) keep the "first_col" layout. In "first_col" mode the B column aligns the fit-stat values on the decimal mark with its coefficients. In "merged" mode the fit-stat values move out of the B column, which aligns its coefficients alone, and the merged values of a model align on the decimal mark among themselves, one centered block under the model (Excel centers each number as it is). Under nested = TRUE the change rows carry their degrees of freedom (F-change prints 7.29 (2, 28)), which widens the B column in the "first_col" layout; "merged" spans them over the model's columns in the engines that merge.

layout

How several models are laid out. "columns" (default) sets them side by side, one group of columns per model. "stacked" sets them one under the other, one panel per model: each panel is the table of that model alone (its default columns, the confidence interval included, its blocks and fit statistics), opened by a row with its label, then by an Outcome row where Stacked layout says. See Multi-model semantics and table_stack(), which stacks tables built separately.

show_re

Mixed models only: TRUE (default) renders the variance components as a Random effects block of rows, FALSE suppresses it. See table_regression_mixed.

re_scale

Mixed models only: "sd" (default) or "variance", the scale of the random-effects rows. See table_regression_mixed.

re_columns

Mixed models only: the cells of the random-effects rows that are displayed, a subset of c("est", "se", "ci"). See table_regression_mixed.

re_test

Mixed models only: "none" (default), "lrt" or "rlrt", a per-term test of the variance components. See table_regression_mixed.

re_ci

Mixed models only: "wald" (default) or "profile", the intervals of the random-effects rows of lmer and glmer fits. See table_regression_mixed. re_scale, re_columns, re_test or re_ci set to other than its default on a table where no model has random effects raises one spicy_ignored_arg warning.

model_labels

Per-model labels used as the column-group spanner above each model's sub-columns (console + gt / flextable / tinytable / Excel / Word renderers). NULL (default) resolves automatically; see Multi-model semantics for the full rule. A character vector of length length(models) overrides. Refused (error) for a single multinomial model: there the column groups are outcome categories, relabeled via outcome_labels (table_regression_categorical).

outcome_labels

The Outcome body row, which names the outcome of each model under the column headers. NULL (default) shows it when the models do not all have the same outcome and the column headers do not name them: models named in the list or by model_labels, or an outcome that several of the models share. Otherwise the title (one outcome) or the column headers (the outcomes of unnamed models, all different) name them, and the row is left out. A character vector of length length(models) forces the row with those values (the spanner stays as "Model 1, ..." unless model_labels is also supplied), a single model included. FALSE removes the row. With layout = "stacked", the row opens each panel, under the same rule, the labels of the panels taking the place of the column headers; a vector gives each panel its label. table_stack() applies the rule to tables built separately, a table built with FALSE taking no row. A multinomial model alone has no Outcome row, its title naming the outcome; in a stack, its panel takes one by this rule, the label once, across its columns. The console, flextable, Word, Excel and tinytable (HTML, LaTeX, Typst) print each label across the columns of its model. gt, which merges no cells of the body, moves the row into the header: each label spans the columns of its model, under the model's name. A stacked gt table and the markdown grid of tinytable keep the label in the first column of the model, so a long label widens that column. For a single multinomial model, the labels of the category spanners; see table_regression_categorical.

stars

Significance asterisks. FALSE (default; the APA Manual 7, Section 7.14, p. 204, prefers exact p-values) – no stars. TRUE – APA cutoffs c("*" = 0.05, "**" = 0.01, "***" = 0.001). A named numeric vector specifies custom thresholds, e.g. c("+" = 0.10, "*" = 0.05, "**" = 0.01, "***" = 0.001). With output = "excel" a marked estimate is written as text ("64.63***" is not a number); the cells with no marker stay numeric.

nested

Whether to inject pairwise change-statistic rows for adjacent models (M2 vs M1, M3 vs M2, ...). FALSE (default) – pure side-by-side display. TRUE – requires identical nobs and identical response variable across all models. Under a non-classical vcov, each pair is tested by a Wald test of the coefficients the current model adds, on that model's matrix, shown as "Wald F-change" or "Wald \(\chi^2\) (change)" by the regime of its coefficient tests. See Hierarchical (nested) model comparison for the rule, the classes it covers and its small-sample caution.

digits

Decimal places for general numeric tokens (b, beta, se, ci, t, f_change, lrt_change, ame, ame_se, weighted_nobs; the Wald change statistics under a robust vcov follow f_change) and for the term-level tests (partial_chi2, partial_f). Default 2L.

p_digits

Decimal places for p-values (p, ame_p, p_change). APA-strict: leading zero stripped, <.001 (or <.0001 etc. depending on p_digits) for small values. Default 3L; at least 1L, as in the descriptive tables. Every *_digits argument is a whole number: a fraction is an error.

effect_size_digits

Decimals for per-coefficient effect sizes (partial_f2, partial_eta2, partial_omega2) and their intervals. Default 2L.

fit_digits

Decimals for variance-explained / model-level effect-size fit stats (r2, adj_r2, r2_change, adj_r2_change, omega2, f2, f2_change, sigma, rmse). Default 2L.

ic_digits

Decimals for information criteria and deviance (AIC, AICc, BIC, deviance, and their _change form). Default 1L.

decimal_mark

The decimal mark, a single character: "." (the default) or "," in most styles; the Lancet style of spicy_style() uses the middle dot. When "," is used, the CI bracket separator switches to "; " automatically to avoid "0,18 [0,07, 0,30]" ambiguity. With output = "excel", a cell that shows one number is a number, under any mark, which shows the decimal separator of the reader's Excel; the mark applies to the text cells (<,001). See Excel output in spicy-package.

align

Numeric column alignment. "decimal" (default) – pre-pad cells so decimal marks line up vertically (publication-style). For CI cells ([LL, UL]) the left bracket, the LL decimal point, the comma separator, the UL decimal point, and the right bracket are independently aligned across rows. "center" and "right" apply the same alignment to every numeric column.

padding

Non-negative integer giving the extra characters added to each data column's auto-computed width when the default print method renders the table. Default 0L (compact – fits more models in the same console / page width). Use 2L (Stata-like) or 4L for a more spacious look. Headers stay centered above the data region regardless of padding.

labels

How the variables are named in the table: the outcome in the title (and above its columns when the models have different outcomes), a numeric term in its row, and a factor in its header. Four forms:

  • labels = FALSE shows the names the model gives them (bmi, age, sex).

  • labels = TRUE shows each variable's label attribute (as set by haven, labelled, or label_from_names()) when it is present, not NA, and not empty, and the name otherwise: "Linear regression: Body mass index", "Age (years)", "Sex:". The attribute is read off the model frame, or off the data the model was fit on where the model frame lost it. Factor levels, interactions, and transformed terms (log(income), poly(age, 2)) are not variables and keep their names, as do the coefficient rows of factor_layout = "flat".

  • labels = c(age = "Age (years)", sexMale = "Men"), a named character vector, gives the variables and rows it names these labels. Every other variable follows options(spicy.var_labels): its name when the option is unset or FALSE, its label attribute when it is TRUE.

  • labels = var_labels(age = "Age in years") gives the variables and rows it names these labels, and every other variable its label attribute, whatever the option says. var_labels() alone is labels = TRUE.

The names are model identifiers, not display text: the outcome, the term labels of stats::terms() ("age", "sex", "age:sex", a factor's term naming its header, an interaction's term its row when it has one row), and the coefficient names ("(Intercept)", "sexMale"; those of an rms fit in the spelling of lm(), "sexMale" for rms's "sex=Male" and "age:sexMale" for "age * sex=Male"), each naming one row. They keep that form whatever the language of the table. Classes with no terms component (nls(), sampleSelection::selection()) are keyed on their coefficient (or parameter) names alone. With several models, a name is looked up in the terms of all of them and lands on the rows where it exists. A name that matches nothing in the table warns (class spicy_unknown_name), with the list of its terms, and is left out, so one vector can still serve every table of a project. The headers of the subordinate blocks (Random effects, Thresholds, Zero-inflation, ...) are set by the package and cannot be relabeled here.

The default reads options(spicy.var_labels), and a TRUE or FALSE typed in the call wins over it. Any other value, NULL included, is an error. A variable label documents the data file; a published table carries the wording you set here. note_labels gives the outcome a shorter label in the title.

note_labels

The label a variable takes where the table names it in a sentence, in the title and in the notes, in place of the one labels gives it: a named character vector, note_labels = c(sex = "sex at birth"), or a var_labels() object, which reads as one. labels can then name a row with a whole question while the note says "Missing values removed: sex at birth (2).". The rows, the column headers and the spanners keep the labels of labels, and so do the title and the notes for a variable note_labels does not name. A name that matches no column warns and is left out, as in labels, and NULL (the default) renames nothing. A note label that another variable of the table shows is an error (class spicy_label_collision): choose another one, or relabel the other variable.

title, note

Override or suppress the auto-built caption / methodological footer. Three modes per argument, those note has in every table function:

  • NULL (default): the package builds the standard caption ("Linear regression on <DV>" / "Hierarchical linear regression on <DV>" / ..., the outcome named by its label in note_labels, else in labels) and a methodological note, one paragraph in the order of every table of the package: what the model is (its family, design, scale of the coefficients, reference categories, ...), the cases a univariable screen fits on, the inference (VCV type, p-adjust method, ...), the glosses of the blocks, then the abbreviations the column headers and the rows of the fit statistics and of the random effects show ("AIC = Akaike information criterion"), defined as the style in force asks (spicy_style(abbreviations = ); under "jama" they open the note on a line of their own), and the sentences of note_add. Under stars, the legend of the stars follows on a line of its own.

  • FALSE: the corresponding banner row is omitted from every output engine, for note the legend of the stars included. Use when the surrounding manuscript provides its own caption / note.

  • character string (length 1): replaces the auto-built text. A title is printed verbatim. A note replaces the general note and is printed as typed (multi-line notes accepted via embedded "\n") after the lead-in of the style, which a string opening with a lead-in of its own does not repeat, the sentences of note_add after it; the legend of the stars stays on its line below, and note = "" keeps that legend alone.

Validation messages, the spanner row, and the in-body change- stat rows are not affected – they belong to the table structure, not to the banner.

note_add

Sentences to add to the note: a character vector of one or more strings, each printed as typed (no period is added) and joined to the note by a space. They close its paragraph, after the definitions of the abbreviations and before the legend of the stars, in every output and in attr(x, "note"), and the sentences the table writes stay. With a string in note, they follow it, so a wrapper can add a house sentence to every table while one table replaces its note. An NA or an empty string is an error, and so is note_add with note = FALSE, which leaves no note to add to.

output

Output type. "default" (a printable spicy_regression_table); "data.frame" (the displayed table with its numbers); "long" (one row per coefficient, broom's names); "tinytable" / "gt" / "flextable" (rich-format tables); "excel" (writes to excel_path); "clipboard" (copies to system clipboard); "word" (writes flextable to word_path).

excel_path

File path for output = "excel", ending in ".xlsx", in a directory that exists. Default NULL (required when output = "excel").

excel_sheet

Sheet name when writing to Excel. NULL (the default) uses "Regression".

clipboard_delim

Field delimiter for output = "clipboard". Default "\t" (tab-separated, pastes cleanly into Excel / Google Sheets / Word). The clipboard payload mirrors the Excel layout (title row, spanner row, header, body, footer note) but is plain text – horizontal rules, cell merging, decimal alignment and the monospace font cannot be encoded in delimited text and are therefore absent from the paste. A cell holding the delimiter itself (a label with a comma under clipboard_delim = ",", or any number under decimal_mark = ","), a double quote or a line break is quoted RFC 4180-style, so the grid survives whatever delimiter you choose.

Paste behavior by target:

  • Excel / Google Sheets: numerics are auto-detected and right-aligned; text cells stay left-aligned. (P-values such as .005 get re-parsed as 0.005 by Excel's auto-format – to preserve the APA leading-zero-dropped display, prefer output = "excel".)

  • Word: the paste is converted to a Word table; all cells start left-aligned. Apply a Table Style (Insert > Table > Design) for APA-style borders, and set right-alignment on numeric columns (Layout > Align Right). For a self-contained Word file with borders and alignment pre-applied, use output = "word" instead.

word_path

File path for output = "word", ending in ".docx", in a directory that exists. Default NULL (required when output = "word"). The Word table inherits the flextable styling (Calibri font, APA borders, decimal-aligned numerics) and adds Word-specific features: an auto-numbered caption ("Table 1: ...", "Table 2: ...") via Word's SEQ field so multiple table_regression() calls in one document number consecutively; a re-printed header row on each page break; row split prevention so a single coefficient row never wraps across two pages; and an APA-styled note line (*Note.* italic prefix per APA Manual 7 §7.14).

R Markdown / Quarto: for embedded use, prefer output = "flextable" (returns the flextable object that knits to docx/HTML/PDF natively). output = "word" writes a standalone .docx file, suited to scripted exports rather than chunk-level rendering.

word_template

Optional path to a custom .docx file used as the template for output = "word". The template's header, footer, page size, margins, and named styles ("Table Caption" in particular) are honored; the table is appended to the template body. Useful for institutional templates with pre-set headers ("APA Style", "Manuscript Submission Template", etc.). Default NULL (uses flextable's stock template).

Customizing the caption appearance: the table caption is tagged with the Word named style "Table Caption". The visual rendering (italic / bold / color / font) follows whatever that style is set to in the docx template. The stock Word template renders "Table Caption" in italic, the type of the APA table title (APA Manual 7 section 7.11, p. 201), where the APA puts the bold table number on its own line above it (section 7.10, p. 200). For a different appearance (Nature-style bold non-italic, APA-strict 2-line bold-number / italic-title, etc.), edit the "Table Caption" style in a docx template and pass it via word_template = "your_template.docx". Style-based delegation keeps the rendered caption consistent with the surrounding document and lets editorial conventions (Nature, APA-strict, journal-specific) be applied without modifying the call site.

style

A journal style: a theme name ("jama", "nejm", "lancet", "annals", "apa", "aer"), a spicy_style() object, or NULL (the default). A style only changes DEFAULTS – any argument you pass explicitly wins over it. Set options(spicy.style = ) for document-wide scope. A theme covers numeric formatting, the word that opens the note and the abbreviations the note defines, not full editorial conformity; ?spicy_style lists the exact rules each one encodes and the official document they come from. An unknown name is an error.

Value

A spicy_regression_table object (a data.frame subclass with classes c("spicy_regression_table", "spicy_table", "data.frame")) when output = "default". The result carries rendering attributes (title, note, align, padding) and provenance attributes (outcome, model_ids) consumed by the print method and the broom methods. For other output values, returns the format-specific object: gt_tbl, flextable, tinytable; for "data.frame" the displayed table as a data.frame (see as.data.frame.spicy_regression_table()); for "long" a tbl_df (model_id, outcome, term, estimate_type, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, statistic, df, df.residual (the second df of an F test, NA elsewhere), p.value, test_type, nobs, r.squared, adj.r.squared, ..., and last partial_type, the hypothesis of a partial row's test, "II" or "III", NA elsewhere); the file path, invisibly, for "excel" and "word"; the table, invisibly, for "clipboard". The two data frames carry the note as printed in attr(x, "note"). With layout = "stacked", the stacked table of table_stack(), whose value is described there.

Pages by model family

This page documents every argument. What is specific to one family of models (its own arguments and the values the shared ones take for it) is on the page of that family:

  • table_regression_mixed: lmer, glmer, glmmTMB, lme and gls fits.

  • table_regression_survival: coxph, survreg, cph and flexsurvreg fits, the RMST and risk-difference columns.

  • table_regression_ordinal: polr, clm and clmm fits.

  • table_regression_categorical: multinom and mlogit fits.

  • table_regression_counts: zeroinfl and hurdle fits, and the zero-inflation, hurdle and dispersion blocks of glmmTMB.

  • table_regression_survey: svyglm, svyolr and svycoxph fits.

  • table_regression_bayesian: stanreg and brmsfit fits.

  • table_regression_robust: lm_robust, iv_robust, ivreg, tobit, rq and fixest fits.

The other families (linear and generalized linear models, additive models, beta regression and sample selection, and the rms fits) follow the rules of this page. GEE fits are described in table_regression_models(), which lists every supported class. The tokens of show_columns and show_fit_stats are on table_regression_tokens.

Vocabulary tokens

show_columns and show_fit_stats take tokens that select what the table shows and in what order. Every token, and the fit statistics of each model class, are on table_regression_tokens.

R-squared of glm and categorical models

Outside least squares there is no variance to partition, and several \(R^2\) measures compete. They answer different questions and give different numbers on the same fit, so the row label names the measure, and a report should too (Long & Freese 2014, p. 126). A threshold quoted for one measure, such as 0.2 to 0.4 for McFadden's, does not carry over to another (Hemmert et al. 2018).

  • "pseudo_r2_tjur", Tjur's coefficient of discrimination: the mean predicted probability of the observations with the event minus that of the observations without it (Tjur 2009). Binomial models only.

  • "pseudo_r2_mcfadden", McFadden's \(R^2\): \(1 - \log L / \log L_0\), the proportional reduction of the log-likelihood from that of the intercept-only model, \(L_0\) (McFadden 1974).

  • "pseudo_r2_nagelkerke", Nagelkerke's \(R^2\): Cox and Snell's \(1 - (L_0 / L)^{2/n}\) divided by its largest possible value, \(1 - L_0^{2/n}\) (Nagelkerke 1991). It is the max-rescaled R-square of SAS and the Nagelkerke R square of SPSS.

  • "r2_deviance", the deviance \(R^2\): \(1 - D / D_0\), the proportional reduction of the deviance from that of the intercept-only model (Cameron & Windmeijer 1997). It lies between 0 and 1, and within a family it cannot decrease when a predictor is added. For a gaussian glm() with the identity link it is the \(R^2\) of lm(). For mgcv::gam and bam fits of the same families (and of mgcv's nb() and tw()), it is the deviance explained of their summary(), as a proportion. Two exceptions follow the glm(): a quasi-binomial GAM is measured on its trials, and the null model of a bam() keeps its offset, which the null deviance of its summary() leaves out.

A GAM (mgcv::gam or bam) shows the \(R^2\) rows of the glm() of its family and link, computed by the same rules and with the same defaults: Tjur's then McFadden's for a logit on a binary outcome, McFadden's for the other binomial, Poisson and nb() GAMs, the deviance \(R^2\) for the continuous families. The likelihood is that of the fitted GAM, smooth terms included, and a GAM without smooth terms gives the numbers of its glm(). For nb(), the intercept-only model re-estimates theta, as for MASS::glm.nb(). Under mgcv's default REML, the theta of an nb() GAM is not the maximum-likelihood one of glm.nb(): method = "ML" gives its numbers. mgcv's other extended families (betar(), ocat(), scat(), ziP(), cox.ph() and the like) have no such row. mgcv reports only an adjusted \(R^2\): it is the "adj_r2" row of a GAM, shown on request, in a table of GAMs or beside an lm(). The "r2" row of a GAM is dashed beside other models, and refused for a table of GAMs.

The smooth terms of a GAM form a Smooth terms (edf) block below its parametric coefficients, one row per term, labeled as summary.gam() labels it (s(age), te(bmi,ped), s(age):sexF). The B column carries the effective degrees of freedom and the p column the p-value of mgcv's approximate test of the term. The SE, CI and statistic cells are dashed: an edf has no standard error, and the chi-square or F of the test has no place under a t or z header. exponentiate leaves the edf as it is, and no star marks it. Under a robust vcov the p-value is dashed too, since mgcv's test rests on its own covariance matrix, and the note says so. tidy() and output = "long" carry the rows with estimate_type = "edf", the reference df in df and the test in statistic and p.value.

The intercept-only model keeps the offset and the weights of the fitted model. For a MASS::glm.nb() fit it re-estimates theta in McFadden's and Nagelkerke's \(R^2\), as Stata's nbreg does, and keeps the theta of the fitted model in the deviance \(R^2\) (Cameron & Windmeijer 1997). By default each model shows the rows of its family:

  • A logit on a binary outcome (0/1, a factor or a logical), a glm() or rms::Glm(), or a binary rms::lrm(): Tjur's \(R^2\), then McFadden's. Tjur's reads on the scale of the predicted probabilities; McFadden's cannot decrease when a predictor is added. An lrm fitted without y = TRUE reads its outcome from the data, as a glm() does; when the data are gone, its Tjur's cell is a dash and the row leaves its default.

  • The other binomial models (probit, cloglog, a grouped response), Poisson and negative binomial models, polr(), clm(), multinom() and an ordinal rms::lrm(): McFadden's \(R^2\), which depends less than Cox and Snell's or Nagelkerke's on the proportion of events (Menard 2000) and is the Pseudo R2 of Stata's estimation output (Long & Freese 2014, p. 126).

  • The continuous families of glm() (gaussian, Gamma, inverse Gaussian, Tweedie): the deviance \(R^2\). McFadden's and Nagelkerke's are refused for them: the log-likelihood of a density changes with the unit of the outcome, so the same model gets other values, even negative ones, when the outcome is rescaled. For a continuous outcome, the likelihood-ratio index can take large values, positive or negative (Cameron & Windmeijer 1997, p. 333).

  • The quasi families have no likelihood and no default row.

A table of several models shows the union of their rows. A row is filled for every model that defines the measure, and dashed for the others. Nagelkerke's \(R^2\) is shown on request only: its rescaling is ad hoc and its values run high (Allison 2014). The deviance \(R^2\) is available on request for Poisson, negative binomial and quasi models, where McFadden's is lower (Cameron & Windmeijer 1997). For a MASS::glm.nb() fit both deviances take the theta of the fitted model. It is refused for binomial, ordinal and multinomial models, where it equals McFadden's.

A binomial model is measured on its individual trials, whatever the layout of its data: a cbind(successes, failures) response, a proportion with the trials as weights, and 0/1 rows weighted by counts give the McFadden, Nagelkerke and Tjur \(R^2\) of the same model fitted to the expanded 0/1 rows. The likelihood is that of the trials, n is their number, and Tjur's means are weighted by them. For every family, the n of Nagelkerke's formula is the sum of the weights. Weights that are counts thus give the values of the expanded data, and non-integer weights give those of the weighted log-likelihood glm() maximizes, which do not change when the weights are rescaled. The n row still counts rows.

Tjur's \(R^2\) depends more than McFadden's on the proportion of events: in a simulated logit with fixed slopes, taking that proportion from 0.50 to 0.05 moves Tjur's from 0.21 to 0.07 and McFadden's from 0.16 to 0.13. It can decrease when a predictor is added (Tjur 2009, p. 370; Allison 2014). It is at least 0 for a logit with an intercept, but a fixed offset can make it negative, and it is shown with its sign. On request it is also computed for the other links, as the same difference of means, although the mean predicted probability equals the proportion of events for a logit with an intercept (Tjur 2009, p. 366), and not in general under the other links.

Multi-model semantics

Pass a single fit or a list() of fits. Multi-model layout draws a centered spanner label above each model's sub-columns:

  • list("Naive" = m1, "Adjusted" = m2) -> spanner labels "Naive" / "Adjusted". Partial naming (list("Naive" = m1, m2)) auto-fills missing slots as "Model <position>".

  • list(m1, m2) (unnamed) -> if all response variables differ, each outcome becomes the spanner label of its model and the redundant Outcome body row is suppressed. The outcome is named as in the title: its name (from formula(fit)[[2]]), or its label attribute under labels = TRUE. If DVs match, the labels default to "Model 1, 2, ...".

  • Models with different outcomes that the spanner labels do not name (named models, or an outcome that several models share) get an Outcome body row under the headers; outcome_labels = FALSE removes it.

  • model_labels = c("A", "B") overrides everything.

A default label is worded in the language of the table (options(spicy.language)), over the columns and in the notes that cite the model; the column names of as.data.frame() and as_structured() keep the English one ("Model 1: B").

Duplicate explicit names in the list are rejected (spicy_invalid_input) – they would silently collide in the internal model_id key. So is a name that collides with the auto-filled label of another slot (list("Model 2" = m1, m2)): two models under one spanner cannot be told apart in the table, nor addressed by inline(). Rename the model, or pass model_labels.

Stacked layout

layout = "stacked" sets the models one under the other, one panel per model, through table_stack(). Each panel is exactly the table table_regression() gives that model alone, with the same arguments: its default columns ("all_b", the confidence interval included), its reference rows, blocks and fit statistics. A row with the label of the model opens each panel: model_labels, else the names of models, else the outcomes when they all differ, else "Model k". The panels share one column header when they have the same columns, and each opens with its own header otherwise (an odds ratio beside a coefficient, a multinomial model with its outcome categories in columns). Models with different outcomes that the labels of the panels do not name open each panel on an Outcome row, under its label row (outcome_labels), as the tables built alone do in table_stack(). vcov and cluster lists give each panel its own estimator. Under nested = TRUE, the change statistics of each model sit in its own panel, labeled "vs" the model before it. The type of each model, its standard errors and the adjustment of its p-values are worded as in the note of the models side by side, each panel named by its label; the other sentences each open with the labels of the panels they concern. A warning or an error names a model as the side-by-side table does. tidy(), glance() and output = "long" return the rows of the models side by side, under a leading panel column, with one exception: under keep or drop, a multinomial model returns the rows its panel shows, selected by its terms as in its table alone ("age"), where side by side the patterns meet terms named with their outcome ("Student: age"). output = "data.frame" binds the data frames of the panels by rows. A keep, drop or show_intercept = FALSE that leaves a panel without a coefficient row is an error: side by side, such a model keeps its fit statistics beside the others.

Inference and standard errors

vcov selects the variance-covariance estimator:

  • "classical" – OLS, or WLS for a weighted fit (lm) / Fisher information (glm).

  • "HC0" to "HC5" – heteroskedasticity-consistent (via sandwich::vcovHC()).

  • "CR0" to "CR3" – cluster-robust with Satterthwaite-corrected df (via clubSandwich::vcovCR()). Requires cluster.

  • "bootstrap" – nonparametric or cluster bootstrap (boot_n replicates).

  • "jackknife" – leave-one-out / leave-one-cluster-out.

For multi-model use, both vcov and cluster accept a single value (recycled to all models) or a list (one per model). The same fit can appear several times with different estimators to compare standard errors side-by-side.

The note names the estimator of each model under the name every class shares, "classical" followed by what it rests on ("classical (OLS)", "classical (Fisher information)" for every fit by maximum likelihood, "classical (model-based)" for lmer, lme and gls), "heteroskedasticity-robust (HC3)" or "cluster-robust (CR2), clusters by id". The test is named once, by a sentence of its own, where it is not read off the class: "P-values: Satterthwaite t-test, cluster-robust df." under "CR0" to "CR3". In a table of several models, a sentence that holds for some of them only opens with their names ("Model 1: P-values: ..."). An rms::Glm with an estimated dispersion keeps the z test rms gives it, where its glm twin is tested on t.

Inferential regimes for lm / glm (B and AME share the same regime):

  • classical, HC* -> t with df.residual (lm). For glm, the test summary() of the model reports: t on the residual degrees of freedom when the dispersion is estimated (gaussian, Gamma, inverse Gaussian, Tweedie, negative.binomial(theta) and the quasi families), z otherwise (binomial, Poisson, MASS::glm.nb).

  • bootstrap, jackknife -> z asymptotic.

  • CR0-CR3 -> t with Satterthwaite-corrected df (B via clubSandwich::coef_test(); Pustejovsky & Tipton 2018). The AME of an lm is a linear contrast of the coefficients whatever the formula (poly(), I(), log(), splines::ns() and interactions included), tested by clubSandwich::linear_contrast() with its own Satterthwaite df. The AME of a glm is computed by marginaleffects under the same variance, and each row takes the Satterthwaite df of the coefficient of the same name (a predictor entered as itself, a factor level). A row without such a coefficient (a transformed predictor, poly(x, 2)) keeps the test of the glm: t on the residual df when the dispersion is estimated, z otherwise. The df differ from one coefficient to the next: show_columns = "df" prints them in a column.

For other classes the t-vs-z axis follows the estimator's native reference distribution (e.g. glmmTMB, survival, ordinal, betareg, mlogit use z; lm, lme, lmer, rms::ols use t).

A single nnet::multinom model sets its outcome categories as column groups; see table_regression_categorical.

Robust SE availability by model class

Not every estimator is defined for every class. A robust vcov the class cannot honor is refused with spicy_unsupported_vcov, instead of a model-based result under a robust label. The values each class accepts, the vcov column of table_regression_models():

Linear and generalized linearnegbinclassical, HC0-HC5, CR0-CR3, bootstrap, jackknife
Linear and generalized linearrlmclassical

Robust, IV, quantile, panellm_robustclassical (the fit's own)
Robust, IV, quantile, paneliv_robustclassical (the fit's own)

"classical" is the model-based variance, or the variance the fit carries for the classes marked so: estimatr and fixest fits keep the estimator they were computed with, a GEE fit its own sandwich, a survey fit its design-based variance, a Bayesian fit its posterior. Why the other tokens are refused, and the backend of each class, is on the page of its family (see Pages by model family); for lm, glm, GEE, gam, betareg and the rms fits, it is below.

lm also takes "CR1S", the full Stata regress, vce(cluster) convention: the CR1S small-sample scaling (equal to sandwich::vcovCL() with type = "HC1") with t(G - 1) inference, G the number of clusters. Use it to reproduce Stata tables; "CR2" (Bell-McCaffrey, Satterthwaite df) remains the recommended modern choice. AER::ivreg() takes it too (see table_regression_robust). "CR1S" is refused for glm with an explanation: Stata's ML commands use a different convention (G/(G-1) scaling, z), so the label would not match Stata output there. For MASS::glm.nb, the sandwich holds theta at its estimate, so robust standard errors can differ by a few percent from software that includes the score of theta.

A GEE fit (geepack::geeglm) is robust by construction: the fit's own sandwich (or jackknife) standard errors, chosen by geeglm's std.err = option and clustered on its id =, are the displayed inference. HC*, CR* and cluster are refused with a pointer to those fit options.

Cluster-robust backends differ by class but are each cross-validated to the field-standard oracle: lm/glm/lmer/lme/ivreg use clubSandwich (CR2 = Bell-McCaffrey, with Satterthwaite df for lm/lme/lmer/ivreg); coxph/cph use the Lin-Wei grouped-dfbeta sandwich (identical to coxph(..., cluster=)); survreg/tobit/gam/polr/clm/betareg/mlogit/multinom and the Poisson and geometric pscl two-part fits use sandwich::vcovCL(). For gam/bam, spicy forms the sandwich itself, from the GLM score and the penalized covariance of the fit, and lets vcovCL() do only the clustering arithmetic: the sandwich methods for these fits are wrong for a free dispersion, a non-canonical link and a non-Gaussian bam(). Extended families other than nb() (betar, ocat, scat, tw, ...) have another score and are refused. For all of these vcovCL() classes, the one estimator is CR1, requested as "CR1"; the other CR* tokens are refused rather than mapped. rms fits use rms::robcov() (which needs the fit's x = TRUE, y = TRUE). The Lin-Wei and robcov() sandwiches have no small-sample factor: their one estimator is requested as "CR0", and the other CR* tokens are refused rather than mapped. A fit already passed through robcov() keeps its variance, which the note names; for an ols it says "sandwich" rather than "Huber", because the fit does not record whether robcov() used Huber's or Efron's method. glmmTMB fits use glmmTMB::sandwich() (see table_regression_mixed). cluster length is one entry per observation, except mlogit (one per choice situation) and censored coxph (one per subject).

How to specify cluster

Three accepted forms, in order of preference:

  1. Formula – cluster = ~region (or cluster = ~region:year for the interaction of two variables). The variables are looked up in model.frame(fit) first, then in the original data argument captured by the fit. Recommended: independent of the dataset's name, composable for multi-way clustering, consistent with sandwich::vcovCL() / clubSandwich::vcovCR().

  2. String – cluster = "region". A single column name resolved the same way as the formula. Convenient but cannot express interactions.

  3. Vector – cluster = df$region. An atomic vector of length nobs(fit). Use this when the cluster key is derived on the fly (cluster = interaction(df$region, df$year), cluster = as.integer(format(df$date, "%Y"))), comes from a different dataset with matching row order, or is otherwise not a column of the model's data.

A bare unquoted name (cluster = region) is not column selection: it is evaluated as an ordinary R variable. If an object region exists in the calling environment, its value is used as the vector form above; if it does not (the typical "unquoted column name" intent), the call fails with a migration error pointing at ~region / "region". Bare-name column selection is deliberately unsupported – it would require non-standard evaluation magic that breaks under programmatic use (function wrapping, dynamic column choice, loops).

For multi-model use, mix forms freely: cluster = list(~region, "region", df$region).

Hierarchical (nested) model comparison

nested = TRUE adds per-pair change statistics as in-table rows (APA Manual 7 Table 7.15, p. 219 / Stata esttab / SPSS Model Summary convention). Each adjacent pair (M2 vs M1, M3 vs M2, ...) contributes one column of change stats; the FIRST model column gets en-dashes (no previous model to compare to). Validation requires identical nobs and identical response variable across all models.

Structural refusals. Four hierarchies carry no valid change statistic whatever their nobs and response, and are refused with spicy_invalid_input rather than rendered with empty or meaningless cells:

  • A REML pair whose fixed effects differ (nlme::lme(method = "REML"), glmmTMB(REML = TRUE)); see table_regression_mixed.

  • Two fixest fits that absorbed different fixed effects; see table_regression_robust.

  • Mixed-effects fits from different engines (lme4, glmmTMB, nlme::lme); see table_regression_mixed.

  • A MASS::rlm hierarchy. M-estimation minimizes a bounded loss on the scaled residuals: it partitions no sums of squares and it is not a likelihood, so there is neither a likelihood-ratio test nor a partial F to report. Every change token is refused – including on a single fit or a nested = FALSE pair, where the token is the explicit request. Compare the least-squares fits (lm()) if the hierarchy itself is the question.

In the first three, nested = FALSE renders the models side by side instead. A hierarchy holding an rms::ols() or rms::lrm() fit estimated with penalty = is rendered side by side, without change statistics and with a warning: neither the partial F nor the likelihood-ratio test is valid for penalized estimates.

Default change tokens auto-injected when show_fit_stats is NULL:

  • All-lm (rms::ols and nls included): c("r2_change", "f_change", "p_change") – APA hierarchical regression standard.

  • All-glm: c("lrt_change", "p_change") – Hosmer, Lemeshow & Sturdivant 2013 Section 2.4; Long & Freese 2014 Section 3.2.4.

  • All-glm whose dispersion is estimated (gaussian, Gamma, inverse Gaussian, Tweedie, quasi families), and the feglm fits of these families: c("f_change", "p_change"), the F test anova(test = "F") reports, \(F = (\Delta D / q) / \hat\phi\) on \((q, df)\), with \(\hat\phi\) the dispersion and \(df\) the residual degrees of freedom of the larger model. "lrt_change" is refused for such a hierarchy.

  • Any other hierarchy that carries a likelihood (survreg, polr, clm, coxph, gls, betareg, multinom, fixest, ...): the same c("lrt_change", "p_change").

  • Mixed-effects: see table_regression_mixed.

  • Quantile (rq): c("f_change", "p_change") – the Wald-type test quantreg::anova.rq() reports.

To customize, pass the change tokens directly to show_fit_stats. The variance-explained change tokens ("r2_change", "adj_r2_change", "f_change", "f2_change") raise spicy_invalid_input on any hierarchy whose nested comparison is a likelihood-ratio test – glm ("f_change" excepted when its dispersion is estimated), and equally every other likelihood class and the mixed-effects families: that comparison reports a chi-square, not a variance-explained change, and the message points at "lrt_change" + "p_change". A quantile hierarchy refuses them too, and "lrt_change" with them, pointing at "f_change" + "p_change" instead. lm, rms::ols and nls keep the least-squares tokens.

The change test follows vcov. Under the classical vcov the change test is the partial F, the likelihood-ratio test, the F test anova() reports for a pair whose dispersion is estimated, or quantreg::anova.rq()'s Wald test, as above. Under any other vcov, and under the classical token when the fit carries a robust variance of its own, it is the Wald test of the coefficients the current model adds, on the matrix its coefficient rows were computed from: \(W = b' V^{-1} b\), with \(b\) the \(q\) added coefficients (aliased ones left out) and \(V\) their block of the matrix. The test takes the regime of the current model's coefficient tests:

  • F, in a row labeled "Wald F-change": \(W / q\) on \((q, df)\) degrees of freedom, the convention of lmtest::waldtest(test = "F") and car::linearHypothesis(). It applies to lm under "HC0"-"HC5" (and "CR1S", on \(G - 1\) degrees of freedom), glm with an estimated dispersion under "HC0"-"HC5", rms::ols under "CR0" or after rms::robcov(), quantreg::rq under "iid" and "ker", and a fixest fit estimated with a non-iid vcov whose coefficient tests are t (on fixest's own degrees of freedom, as fixest::wald()): feols, and feglm with a family whose dispersion is estimated (gaussian, Gamma, inverse Gaussian and the quasi families). Under "CR0"-"CR3", lm, glm (MASS::glm.nb included), lme4::lmer and nlme::lme use the HTZ test of clubSandwich::Wald_test(), the small-sample correction of their coefficient tests.

  • Chi-square, in a row labeled "Wald \(\chi^2\) (change)" that replaces the likelihood-ratio row: \(W\) on \(q\) degrees of freedom, the convention of lmtest::waldtest(test = "Chisq"). It applies to glm with a fixed dispersion and glm.nb under "HC0"-"HC5", lm and glm under "bootstrap" and "jackknife", rq under "bootstrap", glmmTMB under "CR0" and "CR1", under "CR0" to coxph and rms::lrm / cph / Glm, and under "CR1" to survreg, mgcv::gam and bam, polr, clm, betareg, multinom, mlogit, zeroinfl and hurdle (not negative binomial); also to survreg(robust = TRUE), a fixest fit with a non-iid vcov whose coefficient tests are z (fepois, femlm, fenegbin, and feglm with the binomial or Poisson family), and an rms fit of these classes passed through robcov().

\(\Delta R^2\), the information criteria and the deviance change do not depend on the vcov and are unchanged, and a vcov list tests each pair with the current model's estimator. The previous model's coefficients must all appear, under the same names, in the current one, and a smooth term added to a gam under a robust vcov is refused (spicy_invalid_input in both cases). rq keeps anova.rq()'s test under "nid", its default, and under "rank", which yields no matrix. A Wald test of many constraints in a small sample is liberal: on 219 observations, a block of 19 predictors gave F(19, 178) = 6.91 classically and 9.06 as a Wald HC3 test. The HTZ correction under "CR0"-"CR3" mitigates it.

Standardized coefficients

standardized controls the method when "beta" is in show_columns:

  • "refit" – refit on z-scored data. For lm both X and Y are z-scored (Cohen et al. 2003); for glm only numeric X (Long & Freese 2014 Section 4.7.2 "x-standardization").

  • "posthoc" – post-hoc scaling. lm: \(\beta = B \times SD(X) / SD(Y)\); glm: X-only \(\beta = B \times SD(X)\) (Y is undefined on the link scale).

  • "basic" – like "posthoc" but factor dummies are scaled by their column SD.

  • "smart" – Gelman (2008): continuous numeric inputs are scaled by 2 * SD(X) (a +/-1 SD swing then spans the same range as a binary's 0 to 1 step); binary inputs – numeric 0/1 and factor dummies – are left unscaled. (Before 0.13.0 the rule was applied inverted; see NEWS.)

  • "pseudo" – glm only. Menard (2004, 2011) fully-standardized \(\beta = B \times SD(X) / SD(Y^*)\), with \(Y^*\) the latent variable on the link scale and \(SD(Y^*) = \sqrt{Var(\hat{\eta}) + Var_{link}}\) (\(\pi^2/3\) logit, 1 probit, \(\pi^2/6\) cloglog). Binomial families only; non-binomial returns NA with a spicy_caveat.

  • "none" (default) – no \(\beta\) computed.

Interactions and transforms. Under "refit", an interaction's \(\beta\) is the coefficient of the product of the z-scored components – the recommended treatment for such models (Cohen et al. 2003 Section 7.5; Aiken & West 1991; Friedrich 1982). Under "posthoc", "basic", and "smart", the product / transformed design column is treated as a single numeric column and scaled by its own SD (under "smart", by 2 * SD when the product column is continuous; a binary product column – e.g. a binary-by-binary interaction – stays unscaled like any binary input) – the convention of SPSS beta, Stata regress, beta, SAS PROC REG STB, and lm.beta::lm.beta(), identical to effectsize::standardize_parameters(method = "basic") on those columns. The two conventions differ whenever the components are correlated; a spicy_caveat warns and the footer names the convention actually used. "refit" declines formulas with inline transforms (log(x), poly(), factor() written in the formula): the model frame's evaluated columns cannot be re-evaluated on z-scored data, so spicy falls back to "posthoc" with a warning (effectsize's refit instead standardizes before the transform – a different estimand). Pre-build transformed columns in data for an exact refit.

Multiple-comparison adjustment

Adjusting the p-values of all coefficients of a single regression model is not the standard convention. Each coefficient tests a distinct hypothesis on a distinct predictor – not the situation multiple-testing procedures were designed for (Rothman 1990; Greenland 2017; see also Gelman, Hill & Yajima 2012). Hence the default p_adjust = "none".

Adjustment is appropriate for: mass screening with no prior hypothesis (typically "BH" / FDR), pre-registered multi-endpoint confirmatory designs (typically "holm"), or when a journal / SAP explicitly requests it.

The adjustment runs before any keep / drop filtering, so the family is the model's full coefficient set (intercept and reference rows excluded), not the displayed subset – filtering is a display choice and must not change the inferential family.

Output formats and broom integration

output selects the return type:

  • "default" – a spicy_regression_table (data.frame subclass) printed via spicy_print_table().

  • "data.frame" – the displayed table with its numbers, as.data.frame() of the default object: one row per printed row, the key columns variable, label, level and .row_role, then the printed columns, numeric, each interval split into its two bounds.

  • "long" – the long-format tibble, one row per (model_id, term, estimate_type), with broom's column names.

  • "tinytable" / "gt" / "flextable" – rich-format HTML / Word / PDF tables (require the corresponding Suggests package). In a PDF, a "flextable" table wider than the page can be fitted with flextable::fit_to_width().

  • "excel" – writes to excel_path via openxlsx2::wb_save() and returns the path invisibly.

  • "word" – writes to word_path via flextable::save_as_docx() and returns the path invisibly.

  • "clipboard" – copies to the system clipboard via clipr::write_clip().

broom::tidy() returns a long tibble with one row per (model_id, term, estimate_type) and broom-canonical column names (estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high, statistic, p.value). broom::glance() returns one row per model with the model-level statistics; df.residual is kept numeric so cluster-robust Satterthwaite df is preserved.

Global options

  • options(spicy.style = ) – the journal style applied by default to all nine table functions (table_categorical(), table_categorical_svy(), table_continuous(), table_continuous_svy(), table_continuous_lm(), table_outcome(), table_multiresponse(), table_regression() and table_regression_uv()). Takes a theme name ("jama", "nejm", "lancet", "annals", "apa", "aer") or a spicy_style() object. The style of a report is a property of the document, so it is set once in the setup chunk; the style argument overrides it per call, and any formatting argument you type overrides both. options(spicy.style = NULL) restores spicy's own defaults. See spicy_style() for the exact rules each theme encodes and the official document they come from.

  • options(spicy.note_style = ) – how the table note is rendered by the "tinytable" engine (every table function). A note is subordinate to the table it documents, so it is set one size down, in black: 0.9em (\small in LaTeX), matching the "gt" engine and the 10pt-on-11pt of the Word engine. When tinytable::style_tt(fontsize = ) resizes the whole body, the note takes 0.9 of that size. Two opt-ins:

    • "none" – no intervention; the note is rendered exactly as the receiving document template styles it.

    • any other string – extra arguments for the Typst text() call around the note, appended to the size (e.g. options(spicy.note_style = "fill: luma(89)") for a gray note). Typst only: the HTML note keeps its size.

    options(spicy.note_style = NULL) restores the default.

Weights

No weights argument: weights are a property of the fit (extracted via stats::weights()). Pass them when fitting: lm(y ~ x, data = df, weights = w). All downstream computations (vcov, AME, standardization, weighted_nobs) extract them automatically.

Internationalization

Output follows options(spicy.language) (see spicy_labels()); the column names of as.data.frame() and as_structured() stay English in every language. Override user-facing strings via reference_label, model_labels, outcome_labels, and labels. The title and footer are post-processable via attr(result, "title") and attr(result, "note").

Classed conditions

Every error and warning emitted by table_regression() carries a classed condition for programmatic dispatch via tryCatch() or withCallingHandlers(). Errors inherit from spicy_error (root); warnings from spicy_warning. Specific leaves used by this function include spicy_invalid_input, spicy_invalid_data, spicy_unsupported, spicy_unsupported_vcov, spicy_unsupported_standardized, spicy_missing_pkg, spicy_missing_column, spicy_ignored_arg, spicy_caveat, spicy_fallback. See spicy for the full taxonomy.

If a class is not listed there, try table_regression(fit) anyway – unsupported classes error with a clear message. Other regression-table functions: table_stack() to stack regression tables one under the other; table_continuous_lm() for one-predictor-by-many-outcomes descriptive tables. Other spicy table functions: freq(), cross_tab(), table_categorical(), table_continuous(). Underlying machinery: spicy_print_table() for ASCII rendering; build_ascii_table() for the low-level renderer. Inferential infrastructure (internal): compute_model_vcov(), compute_coef_inference(), compute_wald_test(). broom integration: broom::tidy(), broom::glance().

Examples

# ---- Single-model usage ------------------------------------------
fit <- lm(wellbeing_score ~ age + sex + smoking, data = sochealth)

# Default APA layout: B / SE / 95% CI / p plus the n / R^2 /
# Adj. R^2 fit-stats footer. Factor reference level is annotated
# with `(ref.)` and shows an en dash in the statistic columns.
table_regression(fit)
#> Linear regression: wellbeing_score
#> 
#>  Variable        │    B      SE       95% CI        p   
#> ─────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)     │   65.20  1.66  [61.95, 68.45]  <.001 
#>  age             │    0.05  0.03  [-0.01,  0.11]   .130 
#>  sex:            │                                      
#>    Female (ref.) │     –     –          –          –    
#>    Male          │    3.86  0.91  [ 2.08,  5.63]  <.001 
#>  smoking:        │                                      
#>    No (ref.)     │     –     –          –          –    
#>    Yes           │   -1.72  1.11  [-3.89,  0.45]   .121 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌
#>  n               │ 1175                                 
#>  R²              │    0.02                              
#>  Adj. R²         │    0.02                              
#> 
#> Note. Linear regression. Std. errors: classical (OLS). CI = confidence interval.

# \donttest{
# Standardized coefficients (beta) injected next to B. "refit"
# is the Cohen et al. (2003) refit-on-z-scores convention;
# "basic" reproduces the SPSS / Stata regress, beta definition.
table_regression(fit, standardized = "refit")
#> Linear regression: wellbeing_score
#> 
#>  Variable        │    B       β     SE       95% CI        p   
#> ─────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)     │   65.20  -0.10  1.66  [61.95, 68.45]  <.001 
#>  age             │    0.05   0.04  0.03  [-0.01,  0.11]   .130 
#>  sex:            │                                             
#>    Female (ref.) │     –      –     –          –          –    
#>    Male          │    3.86   0.25  0.91  [ 2.08,  5.63]  <.001 
#>  smoking:        │                                             
#>    No (ref.)     │     –      –     –          –          –    
#>    Yes           │   -1.72  -0.11  1.11  [-3.89,  0.45]   .121

# }

# \donttest{
# Custom column set: B + AME + AME-specific p-value. Note that
# the `p` token always belongs to B, never to AME -- use the
# explicit `ame_p` token for AME inference.
if (requireNamespace("marginaleffects", quietly = TRUE)) {
  table_regression(
    fit,
    show_columns = c("b", "p", "ame", "ame_ci", "ame_p")
  )
}
#> Linear regression: wellbeing_score
#> 
#>  Variable        │    B       p     AME      95% CI        p   
#> ─────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────
#>  (Intercept)     │   65.20  <.001                              
#>  age             │    0.05   .130   0.05  [-0.01, 0.11]   .130 
#>  sex:            │

#>  smoking:        │                                             
#>    No (ref.)     │     –     –       –          –         –

#>  n               │ 1175

#>  Adj. R²         │    0.02                                     
#> 
#> Note. Linear regression. Std. errors: classical (OLS). AME of a continuous predictor: average slope (dY/dX). AME = average marginal effect; CI = confidence interval.

# \donttest{
# Group-token shortcut: "all_b" + "all_ame" expands to the full
# B / AME column families side by side.
if (requireNamespace("marginaleffects", quietly = TRUE)) {
  table_regression(fit, show_columns = c("all_b", "all_ame"))
}

# ---- Cluster-robust variance -------------------------------------
# CR2 (Bell-McCaffrey) with Satterthwaite-corrected df is the
# recommended default under few clusters. Three forms are accepted
# for `cluster`; the formula is preferred for composability with
# multi-way clustering and for programmatic robustness.
# \donttest{
if (requireNamespace("clubSandwich", quietly = TRUE)) {
  table_regression(fit, vcov = "CR2", cluster = ~region)
}
#> Linear regression: wellbeing_score
#> 
#>  Variable        │    B      SE       95% CI        p

#>  age             │    0.05  0.04  [-0.05,  0.15]   .285

if (requireNamespace("clubSandwich", quietly = TRUE)) {
  table_regression(fit, vcov = "CR2", cluster = "region")
}

# \donttest{
# ---- Hierarchical (nested) regression ----------------------------
# Adds in-table change-statistic rows (Delta R^2 / F-change /
# p-change for lm; LRT / p-change for glm) below the fit-stats.
# Note: hierarchical comparison requires identical observations
# across all models -- prepare a complete-case subset first so
# R's listwise deletion does not produce different `nobs` per
# model (which the function rejects).
sochealth_cc <- na.omit(
  sochealth[, c("wellbeing_score", "age", "sex", "smoking")]
)
m1 <- lm(wellbeing_score ~ age,                  data = sochealth_cc)
m2 <- lm(wellbeing_score ~ age + sex,            data = sochealth_cc)
m3 <- lm(wellbeing_score ~ age + sex + smoking,  data = sochealth_cc)
table_regression(
  list("Step 1" = m1, "Step 2" = m2, "Step 3" = m3),
  nested = TRUE
)

#> 
#>                           Step 1                     Step 2

#>    Female (ref.) │                           –               –     –

#>

#>  (Intercept)     │   65.20            1.66  <.001

#>    Female (ref.) │     –               –     –

#>    No (ref.)     │     –               –     –    
#>    Yes           │   -1.72            1.11   .121 
#> ╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌┼╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌╌

# The same comparison by its fit statistics alone.
table_regression(
  list("Step 1" = m1, "Step 2" = m2, "Step 3" = m3),
  show_columns = "none",
  nested = TRUE
)

# \donttest{
# ---- Side-by-side variance comparison ----------------------------
# Same fit, three vcovs in one wide table. Useful for showing the
# sensitivity of inference to the variance assumption.
if (requireNamespace("clubSandwich", quietly = TRUE)) {
  table_regression(
    list("Classical" = fit, "HC3" = fit, "CR2" = fit),
    vcov    = list("classical", "HC3", "CR2"),
    cluster = list(NULL, NULL, ~region)
  )
}
